key_discriminator: At Basic level the user searches using simple keywords; at Intermediate they construct deliberate search strategies using Boolean logic and database-specific controlled vocabulary.
what_changes: Shift from reactive keyword entry to proactive strategy design; from single-database to multi-database systematic search; from undocumented to documented search methodology.

false_positives.why_misleading: Google Scholar feels academic and may indicate higher competence, but does not require Boolean searching or database selection skills
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person uses subject headings, proximity operators, or documents their search strategy; Google Scholar-only users are almost always Basic

false_positives.why_misleading: Volume of references suggests extensive searching but may reflect time investment rather than search sophistication
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Check whether references span multiple appropriate databases or are all from a single platform; examine whether search terms are documented

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can correctly apply a Boolean AND query in a subject-relevant database and explain why they chose that database
threshold_evidence.strong: Documented search strategy for a literature review showing multiple databases, Boolean operators, and date/document-type filters

regression_risk: Medium -- search skills atrophy without regular use; researchers who move into non-research roles may regress to basic searching
assessment_difficulty: Medium -- requires direct observation or documented output; self-report is unreliable
ai_context: The boundary is increasingly tested by AI search tools; a student using Elicit with critical evaluation of its limitations may be functioning at Intermediate even without traditional Boolean skills

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the user applies established search strategies; at Advanced they design and validate new search methodologies and teach others.
what_changes: Shift from applying known methods to evaluating and extending them; from searching for one's own research to advising others; from using databases to understanding their indexing architecture and coverage limitations.

false_positives.why_misleading: Fluent multi-database searching may still be application of learned methods rather than critical evaluation of methodology
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person can identify the specific limitations of each database they use and justify their database selection strategy for a novel research question

false_positives.why_misleading: Career stage does not guarantee advanced search competence; many senior researchers use Intermediate-level search skills throughout their careers
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Evidence of teaching search methodology or contributing to systematic review search protocols distinguishes Advanced from Intermediate

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can critique a peer's search strategy, identifying specific methodological weaknesses and suggesting improvements
threshold_evidence.strong: Published or submitted systematic review search protocol with full justification of database and filter choices

regression_risk: Low at Advanced level -- once attained, these skills are stable with minimal use
assessment_difficulty: High -- requires expert peer review; most HE contexts lack assessors with sufficient expertise
ai_context: Advanced searchers are actively integrating AI semantic search tools alongside traditional methods and can articulate when each is appropriate

key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user conducts and teaches expert systematic searching; at Highly Advanced they develop new search methodologies and shape professional discourse.
what_changes: Shift from conducting excellent searches to publishing on search methodology; from teaching within existing frameworks to contributing to framework development; from institutional to sector or international leadership.

false_positives.why_misleading: Professional role suggests high competence but does not guarantee methodological contribution or publication
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for published methodological work, consortium membership, or evidence of shaping practice beyond own institution

false_positives.pattern: High volume of systematic review publications
false_positives.why_misleading: Conducting many systematic reviews demonstrates Advanced competence but not necessarily Highly Advanced unless accompanied by methodological innovation or leadership
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Check whether the person has led methodological development in the field, not just applied existing methods prolifically

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published work that introduces or validates a new search methodology component, adopted or cited by others
threshold_evidence.strong: Leadership of a systematic review methodology consortium, national search guidelines authorship, or invited expert contribution to JRC or EPPI methodology development

regression_risk: Very low -- Highly Advanced competence is sustained by ongoing professional contribution
assessment_difficulty: Very high -- requires assessment by field-level peers with equivalent expertise
ai_context: Highly Advanced searchers are contributing to the emerging methodological literature on AI's role in systematic search and evidence synthesis

key_discriminator: At Basic level evaluation is checklist-driven and surface-level; at Intermediate it is methodologically grounded and engages with research quality criteria.
what_changes: Shift from recognising obvious unreliability to applying structured frameworks; from trusting institutional affiliation to assessing methodological quality; from binary (reliable/unreliable) to nuanced quality assessment.

false_positives.why_misleading: Citing only peer-reviewed sources may reflect instruction-following rather than genuine quality evaluation; the student may not understand why these sources are preferred
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask the student to explain what quality indicators they used and why a specific paper is reliable; Basic users typically cannot articulate methodological reasoning

false_positives.why_misleading: Applying a checklist tool can be done at Basic level by following instructions; genuine Intermediate evaluation involves understanding the reasoning behind criteria
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask the student to evaluate a source not covered by the checklist or to explain why two sources with similar CRAAP scores differ in suitability for a specific purpose

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can identify at least two specific methodological weaknesses in a provided research paper beyond surface features
threshold_evidence.strong: Written critical evaluation of a body of literature demonstrating awareness of study design, sample limitations, and conflicts of interest

regression_risk: Medium -- evaluation skills require active practice; without continued research engagement they may revert toward checklist application
assessment_difficulty: Medium -- requires domain knowledge to assess well; generic assessors may miss discipline-specific quality criteria
ai_context: The BI boundary now includes AI literacy: Intermediate evaluators actively check AI-generated summaries against primary sources, while Basic users may not think to do so

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the evaluator applies quality frameworks correctly; at Advanced they engage with epistemological assumptions and synthesise across contradictory evidence.
what_changes: Shift from applying frameworks to interrogating their assumptions; from evaluating individual studies to synthesising contradictory evidence bodies; from personal research practice to training and advising others.

false_positives.why_misleading: Training in systematic review quality appraisal teaches Intermediate-level tools (CASP, GRADE); Advanced competence requires applying these tools critically and adapting them to novel evidence problems
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess whether the person can handle a case where established quality appraisal tools give misleading results for a specific study type

false_positives.why_misleading: PhD training develops Intermediate evaluation as a standard; Advanced involves contributing to evaluation methodology, not just applying it expertly
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for evidence of advising others, designing quality appraisal processes, or critically engaging with the limitations of appraisal frameworks themselves

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can use a validated quality appraisal tool (GRADE, CASP) on a complex evidence body and explain where the tool's assumptions do not hold for specific studies
threshold_evidence.strong: Published systematic review with full quality appraisal section demonstrating expert handling of contradictory evidence and methodological heterogeneity

regression_risk: Low -- Advanced evaluation skills are durable
assessment_difficulty: Very high -- requires domain-expert peer review to distinguish genuine Advanced from confident Intermediate
ai_context: Advanced evaluators critically assess AI systems as knowledge sources, not just AI-generated content; they evaluate training data provenance, model limitations, and the epistemological status of AI-generated claims

key_discriminator: At Advanced level the evaluator is an expert practitioner; at Highly Advanced they develop new frameworks and shape the scholarly discourse on information evaluation.
what_changes: Shift from expert practice to framework development; from institutional guidance to sector or national policy influence; from applying evaluation theory to generating it.

false_positives.why_misleading: Prolific systematic review publication demonstrates Advanced practice; Highly Advanced requires methodological innovation or leadership
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for methodological papers, framework development, or contributions to evidence synthesis standards bodies

false_positives.why_misleading: Academic seniority correlates with but does not define Highly Advanced evaluation competence
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess scholarly contribution to the field of evidence evaluation specifically, not general academic seniority

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published work that advances the methodology or theory of information evaluation, adopted or cited by other practitioners
threshold_evidence.strong: Membership of systematic review methodology consortium, authorship of national evidence standards, or published theory of knowledge evaluation in AI-mediated environments

ai_context: At this level, individuals are publishing on what rigorous information evaluation means when AI mediates much of our access to and representation of knowledge

key_discriminator: At Basic level information is saved informally without a retrieval system; at Intermediate a deliberate reference management and personal knowledge management system is in place.
what_changes: Shift from ad hoc saving to systematic organisation; from manual citation formatting to reference management software; from individual documents to project-structured knowledge systems.

false_positives.why_misleading: Accumulation without retrieval strategy is not management; large unorganised archives are a Basic-level artefact despite representing significant digital activity
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask the person to locate a specific paper from six months ago in under two minutes; inability to do so efficiently indicates Basic information management regardless of volume

false_positives.why_misleading: Cloud storage is infrastructure, not an information management system; presence of cloud storage does not indicate Intermediate competence
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess the folder structure, naming conventions, and whether a reference manager is integrated

threshold_evidence.minimum: Consistent use of reference management software (Zotero, Mendeley, EndNote) with organised folders and tags for a research project
threshold_evidence.strong: Research project with documented search-to-management workflow: database search connected to reference manager, annotated bibliography, organised folder structure

regression_risk: High -- information management habits are fragile without consistent practice; researchers not currently engaged in intensive literature work may revert to ad hoc saving
assessment_difficulty: Low -- directly observable through portfolio review, dissertation bibliographies, and reference manager sharing
ai_context: The BI boundary now includes how AI outputs are managed: Intermediate users integrate AI tool outputs into their reference management system with provenance documentation

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the user manages their own research information well; at Advanced they design systems for others and address funder/institutional data management requirements.
what_changes: Shift from personal information management to team and project data management; from reference organising to research data management planning; from individual knowledge systems to shared institutional repositories.

false_positives.pattern: Experienced postgraduate researcher with tidy reference manager
false_positives.why_misleading: Excellent personal information management can plateau at Intermediate without the extension to team, institutional, and funder data management contexts
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has created a Data Management Plan or managed a shared team research library; absence of these indicates Intermediate rather than Advanced

false_positives.pattern: Using institutional repository for publication deposit
false_positives.why_misleading: Depositing publications is basic open access compliance; Advanced management involves contributing metadata quality, onboarding team members, and managing complex data governance
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess whether the person understands FAIR principles and can apply them to a complex dataset beyond publications

threshold_evidence.minimum: DPIA or Data Management Plan submitted for a research project, demonstrating understanding of storage, sharing, and retention requirements
threshold_evidence.strong: Funder-compliant research data management workflow for a completed project, including documentation of data organisation, sharing, and preservation according to FAIR principles

regression_risk: Low -- Advanced management skills, once applied, are sustained by funder and institutional requirements
assessment_difficulty: Medium -- DMP quality can be assessed by research data specialists
ai_context: Advanced managers treat AI-generated outputs as a formal data type in their research data management framework, with provenance documentation and retention policies

key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user implements excellent data management; at Highly Advanced they shape the infrastructure and policy that others use.
what_changes: Shift from implementing data management plans to designing institutional data management infrastructure; from FAIR compliance to FAIR infrastructure development; from local to national/international standards contribution.

false_positives.why_misleading: The job title suggests Advanced competence but Highly Advanced requires shaping national or international standards or infrastructure, not just excellent local implementation
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for contributions to RDMF, DCC, RDA, or equivalent international research data management bodies

false_positives.why_misleading: Excellent data publication practice is Advanced; Highly Advanced involves contributing to the FAIR framework itself or to institutional infrastructure that enables others to achieve FAIR compliance
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess scholarly contribution to data management standards, not just compliance with them

threshold_evidence.minimum: Institutional open research data policy authored or contributed to, with evidence of implementation and adoption
threshold_evidence.strong: Published contribution to international research data infrastructure standards or governance (RDA working group, DCC guidance, OpenAIRE) with demonstrable sector impact

ai_context: Highly Advanced information managers are shaping institutional policy on AI-generated data as a distinct data type with its own provenance, quality, and retention challenges

competency_name: Interacting through and with digital technologies
key_discriminator: At Basic level the user participates in digital communication when given a link or prompt; at Intermediate they select channels strategically and facilitate digital interactions.
what_changes: Shift from reactive participation to proactive channel selection; from joining meetings to facilitating them; from using provided communication structures to designing them.

false_positives.why_misleading: Frequent communication does not indicate strategic channel selection or facilitation capability
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess whether the person makes deliberate choices between email, Teams chat, video call, and async document based on communication type and audience

false_positives.why_misleading: Comfortable video call use is achievable at Basic level; Intermediate involves managing the meeting, not just attending
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask for evidence of organising and facilitating an online meeting, not just attending one

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can explain why they would choose different channels for a time-sensitive urgent message vs a complex discussion vs a permanent record
threshold_evidence.strong: Evidence of facilitating a synchronous online session with multiple participants, managing turn-taking and follow-up

regression_risk: Low -- interaction skills are reinforced by daily practice
assessment_difficulty: Medium -- observable through meeting participation and communication artefacts
ai_context: The BI boundary includes AI communication tool awareness: Intermediate users actively use AI meeting summaries and AI-assisted translation while maintaining awareness of their limitations

competency_name: Interacting through and with digital technologies
key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the user is an effective digital communicator; at Advanced they design communication systems and critically evaluate tool implications.
what_changes: Shift from effective participation to system design; from using communication tools to evaluating them critically for their organisational, ethical, and accessibility implications.

false_positives.pattern: Heavy Teams or Slack power user
false_positives.why_misleading: Advanced tool fluency may still be sophisticated application rather than critical design of communication architecture
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has designed a communication protocol for a team, not just used existing channels effectively

false_positives.why_misleading: Feature training is an Intermediate activity; Advanced communication expertise involves designing the overall communication environment, not just specific tool features
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for evidence of designing communication norms, channel structures, and policy contributions, not just tool tutorials

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has authored a communication protocol or digital working agreement for a team that includes rationale for channel and tool choices
threshold_evidence.strong: Institutional communication policy contribution that addresses accessibility, data protection implications, and AI communication tool governance

ai_context: Advanced communicators critically evaluate AI features in communication platforms (auto-summaries, AI-moderated discussions) for appropriateness and accuracy before institutional adoption

competency_name: Interacting through and with digital technologies
key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user designs excellent communication environments; at Highly Advanced they shape sector norms and contribute to scholarly or policy discourse.
what_changes: Shift from institutional leadership to sector influence; from designing systems to publishing on or regulating the systems others design.

false_positives.why_misleading: Institutional leadership demonstrates Advanced practice; Highly Advanced requires sector or scholarly contribution beyond the institution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for published work, policy contributions, or standards body involvement

false_positives.why_misleading: Network size is not competence; the quality and influence of scholarly or policy contribution matters
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess publication or policy contribution record rather than social network metrics

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published or widely cited framework on digital communication in HE, or formal advisory contribution to national communication policy
threshold_evidence.strong: Scholarly publication on AI-mediated communication ethics, accessibility standards contribution, or regulatory advisory role

ai_context: Highly Advanced practitioners are contributing to the discourse on what AI-mediated communication means for human connection, authenticity, and professional accountability in HE

key_discriminator: At Basic level content is shared with permission controls applied; at Intermediate licences are understood and applied, and open sharing is practised.
what_changes: Shift from managed sharing to licensed open sharing; from knowing sharing exists to selecting appropriate licence types; from compliance to proactive open access practice.

false_positives.why_misleading: Access control is Basic-level sharing competence; Intermediate involves understanding licences for open sharing beyond institutional boundaries
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person understands the difference between CC BY and CC BY-NC-ND and when they would choose each

false_positives.why_misleading: Uploading to ResearchGate may be done without awareness of the legal or licensing implications
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person selected a licence, checked publisher embargo, or understood green vs gold open access before uploading

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can correctly select and apply a Creative Commons licence to an original piece of work and explain what permissions it grants
threshold_evidence.strong: Open access publication deposited in institutional repository with correct licence and funder compliance documentation

regression_risk: Medium -- licence knowledge requires periodic updating as funder mandates evolve
assessment_difficulty: Medium -- licence practice is observable through deposit records
ai_context: The BI boundary includes AI output sharing: Intermediate sharers understand that sharing AI-assisted work requires disclosure and appropriate licence consideration

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the user shares their work correctly; at Advanced they advise others and design open sharing strategies.
what_changes: Shift from personal compliance to institutional strategy; from selecting licences to advising on complex licence scenarios; from following mandates to designing data sharing workflows.

false_positives.why_misleading: Personal open access compliance is Intermediate; Advanced involves strategic design and advising others across complex scenarios
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person advises others on publisher agreements, embargo management, or FAIR data sharing; if not, they are Intermediate

false_positives.why_misleading: Data deposit is good practice at Intermediate; Advanced involves understanding the FAIR principles in depth, negotiating data sharing agreements, and navigating privacy constraints
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask about a scenario involving personal data in a dataset -- Advanced practitioners navigate anonymisation, consent, and sharing restrictions; Intermediate practitioners may not

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can advise a colleague on the correct open access route for a paper with a specific funder requirement, including embargo and self-archiving options
threshold_evidence.strong: FAIR-compliant research data package with full metadata, licence, and sharing documentation for a complex dataset

ai_context: Advanced sharers navigate the evolving norms for sharing AI-assisted research outputs, including attribution and licence implications of AI-generated components

key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user implements expert open sharing; at Highly Advanced they shape international open science infrastructure and policy.
what_changes: Shift from implementing excellent practice to building the infrastructure and governance that others rely on.

false_positives.why_misleading: Operational repository management is Advanced; Highly Advanced involves governance of open science standards and infrastructure beyond one institution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for ORCID governance participation, DataCite or OpenAIRE involvement, or scholarly contribution to open science policy

false_positives.why_misleading: Volume demonstrates practice; Highly Advanced requires sector shaping
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess scholarly contribution to open science standards rather than quantity of deposits

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published scholarly work on open science governance or formal contribution to international open science infrastructure
threshold_evidence.strong: Governance role in OpenAIRE, DataCite, Creative Commons, or equivalent international open science infrastructure

ai_context: Highly Advanced practitioners are shaping the policy response to AI and open science: what provenance, attribution, and reproducibility standards are needed when AI mediates knowledge creation

competency_name: Engaging in citizenship through digital technologies
key_discriminator: At Basic level the user participates in digital civic activities when prompted; at Intermediate they engage critically and contribute proactively to digital civic spaces.
what_changes: Shift from passive participation to active, critical engagement; from completing surveys to contributing to consultations; from following institutional channels to critically evaluating civic digital information.

false_positives.why_misleading: Social media activity is not civic participation; Intermediate digital citizenship involves contributing to governance processes, not social broadcasting
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask for examples of contributing to institutional consultations, professional body governance, or civic technology initiatives

false_positives.why_misleading: Membership is Basic; active participation in student union digital governance and contributing to institutional decision-making is Intermediate
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has responded to consultations or contributed to governance processes, not just attended events

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has submitted a response to an institutional or professional consultation through digital channels and can explain the process
threshold_evidence.strong: Active engagement with professional community digital platforms showing constructive contribution to field-relevant discussions

regression_risk: Medium -- civic digital engagement requires ongoing motivation
ai_context: Intermediate citizens recognise AI-generated civic content and apply critical evaluation to algorithmically curated civic information

competency_name: Engaging in citizenship through digital technologies
key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the user is an active digital citizen; at Advanced they design and facilitate digital civic engagement initiatives.
what_changes: Shift from participation to facilitation and advocacy; from engaging in civic digital spaces to designing and improving them.

false_positives.why_misleading: Public digital commentary is a form of digital citizenship but not the same as designing inclusive civic participation processes
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask for evidence of facilitating or designing a civic participation process, not just contributing to public discussion

false_positives.why_misleading: Responding to consultations is Intermediate; Advanced involves designing consultations and advocacy for inclusive participation
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for leadership of participation processes, design of engagement tools, or advocacy work

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has designed or facilitated a digital civic engagement process with attention to inclusivity and documented outcomes
threshold_evidence.strong: Published policy response, advocacy campaign, or research contribution on digital civic participation in HE

ai_context: Advanced digital citizens advocate for AI-literate democratic participation and contribute to discourse on AI and democratic integrity

competency_name: Engaging in citizenship through digital technologies
key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user is a civic engagement leader; at Highly Advanced they shape national or international policy on digital democracy.
what_changes: Shift from institutional leadership to sector or national policy influence.

false_positives.why_misleading: Building civic tech tools is Advanced; Highly Advanced involves shaping the governance and regulatory framework for digital civic participation
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for policy advisory roles, published scholarship, or formal regulatory contribution

false_positives.why_misleading: Institutional seniority in civic engagement is Advanced; sector or national influence distinguishes Highly Advanced
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess national or international policy contribution rather than institutional role

threshold_evidence.minimum: Formal contribution to national digital democracy policy or published scholarship on digital civic participation in HE
threshold_evidence.strong: Advisory panel membership for digital democracy, AI regulation, or civic technology governance at national or international level

ai_context: At this level individuals are shaping national policy on AI and democratic participation

key_discriminator: At Basic level collaboration tools are used when set up by others; at Intermediate the user coordinates digital projects and establishes collaborative norms.
what_changes: Shift from participation to coordination; from using shared tools to setting up and managing collaborative workflows and norms.

false_positives.why_misleading: Using shared documents is Basic; Intermediate involves coordinating workflows and establishing team norms around collaborative tools
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has set up a project management system or established collaborative working agreements for a team

false_positives.why_misleading: Daily platform use is Basic; Intermediate coordination involves deliberate workflow design and task management
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask for evidence of using a project management tool (Trello, Asana, MS Planner) to coordinate a team task with deadlines and responsibilities

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can set up and manage a collaborative project space (shared document library, task board) for a small team and onboard others
threshold_evidence.strong: Project management board or documented workflow showing coordinated multi-person task completion across an asynchronous team

ai_context: Intermediate collaborators are establishing team norms for AI tool use in collaborative work including attribution and quality checking

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the user coordinates digital collaborations; at Advanced they design collaboration environments and lead complex interdisciplinary projects.
what_changes: Shift from coordinating to designing; from single-team collaboration to leading complex interdisciplinary or international projects.

false_positives.why_misleading: Operational coordination competence may plateau at Intermediate; Advanced design involves selecting and configuring tools for specific collaboration goals and managing interdisciplinary complexity
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has designed a collaboration environment from scratch for a specific project goal, including tool selection rationale and accessibility considerations

false_positives.why_misleading: High publication collaboration demonstrates research network engagement but not necessarily advanced digital collaboration design
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask about the collaboration infrastructure used -- did they design it or use what was given?

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has designed a digital collaboration environment for a research team or educational cohort with documented rationale for tool selection and configuration
threshold_evidence.strong: Leadership of an interdisciplinary or international collaborative research project with documented collaboration infrastructure and evaluation

ai_context: Advanced collaborators design ethical AI-human collaborative environments with explicit norms for attribution and quality assurance

key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user leads complex collaborations; at Highly Advanced they shape the infrastructure and policy that enables digital collaboration at scale.
what_changes: Shift from project leadership to infrastructure development and sector influence.

false_positives.why_misleading: Leading international research collaborations is Advanced; Highly Advanced involves contributing to the infrastructure and standards others use
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for contributions to open science platforms, collaborative research standards, or scholarly work on the future of digital collaboration

false_positives.why_misleading: Volume of collaboration does not indicate infrastructure contribution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess contribution to collaboration tools, standards, or sector guidance rather than project count

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published scholarly contribution to the theory or practice of digital collaboration in HE, or formal contribution to a national/international collaboration platform or standard
threshold_evidence.strong: Leadership of a major open science infrastructure project or widely adopted collaboration framework for HE research

ai_context: Highly Advanced practitioners shape norms for human-AI collaborative knowledge production in research

key_discriminator: At Basic level the user avoids obvious digital misconduct; at Intermediate they understand and can articulate institutional policy and model positive digital behaviour.
what_changes: Shift from avoiding obvious violations to actively modelling and explaining institutional norms; from reactive (don't do bad things) to proactive (actively cultivate positive digital culture).

false_positives.why_misleading: Absence of complaints indicates Basic avoidance; Intermediate involves active modelling of positive norms and ability to support others
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person can explain the reasoning behind institutional digital conduct policies and has helped others navigate conduct challenges

false_positives.why_misleading: Good personal behaviour is Basic; Intermediate includes supporting and modelling for others in shared digital spaces
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for evidence of addressing a conduct issue constructively or helping establish ground rules for a digital collaborative space

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can explain institutional digital conduct policies, their rationale, and apply them to a non-obvious case scenario
threshold_evidence.strong: Evidence of constructively addressing a digital conduct situation or helping a peer group establish positive digital norms

ai_context: Intermediate digital behaviour includes understanding and applying institutional AI use policies and recognising AI-enabled misconduct

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the user models good behaviour and applies policy; at Advanced they design and deliver training and contribute to policy development.
what_changes: Shift from personal practice to institutional contribution; from following policy to shaping it.

false_positives.pattern: Module tutor who sets digital ground rules
false_positives.why_misleading: Setting ground rules for a class is Intermediate; Advanced involves designing institutional frameworks and training programmes that work at scale
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has designed a training programme or policy document for digital behaviour that has been adopted institutionally

false_positives.why_misleading: Personal commitment is Intermediate; Advanced involves institutional contribution to integrity policy and culture
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for policy authorship, training programme design, or institutional leadership contributions

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has designed and delivered a digital behaviour or AI integrity training programme for an institutional audience
threshold_evidence.strong: Contribution to institutional digital conduct policy, social media guidelines, or AI use policy with evidence of adoption

ai_context: Advanced practitioners design AI behaviour frameworks for their institutions covering disclosure, impersonation, and the integrity implications of AI-assisted communication

key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user is an institutional digital culture leader; at Highly Advanced they shape national or international discourse on digital behaviour ethics.
what_changes: Shift from institutional to sector or scholarly influence.

false_positives.why_misleading: Professional community involvement is Advanced; Highly Advanced involves published scholarship or formal policy contribution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for peer-reviewed publications, government advisory roles, or national standards contributions

false_positives.why_misleading: Institutional seniority in this area is Advanced; national or international discourse contribution distinguishes Highly Advanced
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess publication and policy contribution beyond institution

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published scholarly work on digital behaviour, online harm, or AI ethics in HE, or formal advisory contribution to sector-level digital conduct standards
threshold_evidence.strong: Advisory role with Online Safety regulator, ICO, AI governance body, or equivalent national/international authority on digital conduct

ai_context: At this level individuals shape regulatory frameworks for AI-enabled online harm and the obligations of HE institutions to protect their communities

key_discriminator: At Basic level identity is managed by maintaining institutional profiles; at Intermediate a proactive, strategic digital identity is constructed and maintained across professional platforms.
what_changes: Shift from maintaining assigned profiles to constructing strategic professional identity; from reactive to proactive identity management; from institutional to cross-platform identity curation.

false_positives.why_misleading: Having a LinkedIn profile meets a basic threshold; Intermediate involves strategic, consistent, and regularly curated professional identity across multiple relevant platforms
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Check whether the profile is current, actively managed, and part of a coherent cross-platform professional identity strategy

false_positives.why_misleading: Creating an ORCID is an entry-level action; Intermediate involves actively maintaining it, connecting publications, and using it in professional contexts
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask when the ORCID was last updated and how it is integrated into the researcher's professional workflow

threshold_evidence.minimum: Maintains an active, strategically curated professional identity across at least two relevant platforms (ORCID + LinkedIn, or equivalent), updated within the past 6 months
threshold_evidence.strong: Evidence of a deliberate digital presence audit and privacy management review, with a strategic narrative consistency across institutional and professional platforms

regression_risk: Medium -- digital identity requires ongoing curation
assessment_difficulty: Low -- directly observable through profile review
ai_context: Intermediate users begin managing their AI-generated digital identity: checking how AI search and recommendation systems represent them and taking steps to ensure accuracy

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the user manages their own digital identity; at Advanced they manage complex, multi-audience identities and advise others.
what_changes: Shift from personal management to strategic multi-audience navigation and advising; from maintaining profiles to managing reputation, boundaries, and complex identity situations.

false_positives.why_misleading: Multi-platform presence is Intermediate; Advanced involves strategic navigation of complex identity situations (institutional vs personal boundary management, public intellectual role)
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has navigated a complex identity situation (responding to a reputational challenge online, managing the boundary between institutional and personal digital voice) and how they approached it

false_positives.why_misleading: General career advice may not include digital identity coaching; Advanced identity competence involves specifically advising on digital presence, platform choice, and privacy management for academic and professional contexts
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask for specific examples of advising on digital identity development, not just generic career coaching

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has advised a student or colleague through a digital identity development process including platform choice, content strategy, and privacy management
threshold_evidence.strong: Evidence of strategic management of a complex digital identity across public, professional, and institutional audiences, including navigating a reputational or boundary challenge

ai_context: Advanced identity managers actively monitor and manage how AI systems represent them and contribute to institutional guidance on AI-generated digital identity

key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user manages complex digital identities and advises others; at Highly Advanced they shape institutional and sector policy on digital identity governance.
what_changes: Shift from expert practice to policy influence and scholarly contribution.

false_positives.why_misleading: Commercial digital identity consulting is Advanced; Highly Advanced involves scholarly contribution to or institutional governance of digital identity frameworks
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for published work on digital identity governance, data rights, or AI profiling in academic or policy contexts

false_positives.pattern: Senior HR leader with digital identity policy remit
false_positives.why_misleading: Institutional policy responsibility is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires sector or national influence
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess national or international contribution

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published scholarly work or policy contribution on digital identity governance, algorithmic profiling, or data rights in HE
threshold_evidence.strong: Leadership of an institutional or sector-wide digital identity governance initiative, or formal advisory contribution to GDPR, AI Act, or data rights policy

ai_context: At this level individuals shape the rights framework for AI-generated digital identity, including contestability, accuracy obligations, and governance standards

key_discriminator: At Basic level digital content is created using templates for required tasks; at Intermediate purposeful, accessible content is produced for real audiences using appropriate formats.
what_changes: Shift from task completion to audience-oriented communication; from template use to format selection; from production to accessible, purpose-driven design.

false_positives.why_misleading: Good-looking coursework may be template-based and not reflect independent format selection or accessibility awareness
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person can explain why they chose the format and what accessibility features they applied; absence of accessibility consideration indicates Basic

false_positives.why_misleading: Personal social media content production is not the same as producing purposeful professional or educational digital content
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask for examples of producing digital content for a specific institutional or professional audience, with documented audience consideration and format justification

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has produced a piece of digital content (video, infographic, interactive resource) for a specific real audience with documented format choice rationale and accessibility features applied
threshold_evidence.strong: Digital portfolio or e-learning resource demonstrating consistent application of accessibility guidelines (alt text, captions, contrast) across multiple content types

ai_context: The BI boundary includes AI content tool awareness: Intermediate creators use AI generation tools with critical evaluation of accuracy, bias, and disclosure requirements

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the user produces quality accessible content; at Advanced they lead complex production projects and develop institutional standards.
what_changes: Shift from individual production to project leadership; from following standards to developing them; from creating for one's own audience to designing for institutional or public contexts.

false_positives.why_misleading: Excellent personal content production is Intermediate; Advanced involves leading production projects, coordinating teams, and contributing to institutional content standards
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has led a multi-person content production project or contributed to institutional content quality frameworks

false_positives.why_misleading: Creating e-learning modules is achievable at Intermediate; Advanced involves systematic quality assurance, accessibility auditing, and coordinating specialist contributors
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask about the production process: was it solo or coordinated? Was it formally accessibility-tested? Was it evaluated against pedagogical quality criteria?

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has led a complex digital content production project involving multiple contributors with documented quality assurance and accessibility processes
threshold_evidence.strong: Institutional e-learning course or OER with formal accessibility audit, pedagogical quality review, and evidence of real audience impact

ai_context: Advanced content producers design institutional AI content policies addressing disclosure, quality standards, and pedagogical integrity for AI-assisted production

key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user leads institutional content production; at Highly Advanced they shape the field through scholarly contribution and sector leadership.
what_changes: Shift from institutional leadership to sector influence and scholarly contribution.

false_positives.why_misleading: Contributing many OERs is Advanced practice; Highly Advanced involves shaping OER policy and infrastructure or publishing scholarly work on digital content design
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for national OER leadership, scholarly publication on digital pedagogy, or framework development

false_positives.why_misleading: Excellent individual content is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires sector influence beyond the quality of individual outputs
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess scholarly and policy contribution rather than individual output quality

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published research or sector-leading resource on digital content design in HE, or leadership of a national OER initiative
threshold_evidence.strong: UNESCO OER-aligned contribution, scholarly publication on AI and digital content production in education, or national digital curriculum policy contribution

ai_context: Highly Advanced content practitioners are shaping the scholarly discourse on AI and human creativity in educational content production

key_discriminator: At Basic level existing content is combined; at Intermediate it is synthesised and re-elaborated with original analytical contribution.
what_changes: Shift from collation to synthesis; from combining to transforming; from descriptive to analytical integration of sources.

false_positives.pattern: Long essays drawing on many sources
false_positives.why_misleading: Volume of sources does not indicate synthesis; many long essays are at Basic level because they describe rather than integrate
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Check whether the student's own analysis connects the sources or whether each source is treated in isolation

false_positives.why_misleading: Correct attribution is a Basic behaviour; Intermediate synthesis involves transformative intellectual contribution, not just accurate reference management
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask the student to explain what they added to the sources they used; Intermediate users can articulate their synthesising contribution

threshold_evidence.minimum: A literature review or synthesis report that demonstrably goes beyond description to construct an original analytical framework connecting multiple sources
threshold_evidence.strong: Adapted educational resource based on multiple OERs with documented adaptation rationale and added pedagogical value beyond the source materials

ai_context: Intermediate users use AI synthesis tools with critical evaluation and explicit documentation of AI's contribution to the integration process

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the user produces quality synthesis; at Advanced they conduct rigorous evidence synthesis with methodological sophistication.
what_changes: Shift from analytical synthesis to methodologically rigorous evidence synthesis; from individual research practice to team and institutional knowledge production.

false_positives.why_misleading: High-quality narrative literature reviews are Intermediate; Advanced requires systematic methodology including quality appraisal and reproducible synthesis
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the review used a formal quality appraisal tool (CASP, GRADE), documented inclusion criteria, and could be reproduced by another researcher following the methods

false_positives.why_misleading: Published narrative reviews may be advanced within their discipline but not constitute Advanced re-elaboration unless they demonstrate systematic methodology
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Check for methodological rigour indicators: PROSPERO registration, PRISMA reporting, formal quality appraisal

threshold_evidence.minimum: Evidence synthesis using a formal quality appraisal framework with documented methodology that could be reproduced by another researcher
threshold_evidence.strong: Published or registered systematic review or meta-analysis with full PRISMA reporting and formal quality appraisal

ai_context: Advanced re-elaborators document AI tool contributions to synthesis processes with explicit methodological transparency

key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user conducts expert evidence synthesis; at Highly Advanced they shape synthesis methodology itself.
what_changes: Shift from conducting systematic reviews to developing the methodology others use for conducting them.

false_positives.why_misleading: Prolific systematic review production demonstrates Advanced practice; Highly Advanced requires methodological contribution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for published methodology papers, consortium leadership, or Cochrane/Campbell Collaboration involvement

false_positives.why_misleading: Leading systematic review teams is Advanced; Highly Advanced involves contributing to the standards and methods the field uses
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess methodological publication record and professional community leadership

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published methodological contribution to evidence synthesis, adopted or cited by other practitioners or teams
threshold_evidence.strong: Cochrane, Campbell, EPPI-Centre, or equivalent consortium membership with methodological contribution; or published epistemological work on AI and evidence synthesis

ai_context: Highly Advanced synthesis experts are shaping the epistemological and methodological standards for AI-assisted evidence synthesis

key_discriminator: At Basic level copyright is avoided through attribution; at Intermediate licence types are understood and applied correctly.
what_changes: Shift from attribution-as-compliance to licence selection and application; from avoiding infringement to enabling appropriate reuse through correct licensing.

false_positives.why_misleading: Attribution practice is Basic; Intermediate requires understanding of licence types, not just citation norms
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person knows the difference between CC BY and CC BY-NC and when they would choose each for their own work

false_positives.pattern: Images sourced from Unsplash or Pexels
false_positives.why_misleading: Using free image sites is a Basic strategy; Intermediate copyright competence requires understanding the specific licence conditions of each platform and verifying them at source
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person checked the specific licence for each image and whether they understand what commercial vs non-commercial means in that context

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can correctly apply a CC licence to original work and explain the conditions it places on reuse; can identify the licence of a third-party resource and explain whether and how it can be adapted
threshold_evidence.strong: Work published with correct CC licence choice with documented rationale; evidence of navigating an institutional licence for teaching material use

regression_risk: Medium -- licence knowledge requires updating as mandates evolve
ai_context: The BI boundary now includes awareness of AI copyright ambiguity: Intermediate users understand that the status of AI-generated content is unsettled and seek institutional guidance before sharing

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the user applies licences correctly; at Advanced they advise on complex copyright situations and contribute to institutional policy.
what_changes: Shift from personal licence compliance to advising on complex scenarios and institutional policy contribution.

false_positives.pattern: All work published open access with CC
false_positives.why_misleading: Personal open access compliance is Intermediate; Advanced involves advising on complex scenarios including co-authored works, AI-assisted content, and student IP
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Present a complex scenario (student IP, AI-generated content, co-authored work with multiple licence types) and assess whether the person can navigate it or seeks specialist advice

false_positives.why_misleading: Formal training is valuable context but Advanced competence requires practical application in complex real-world scenarios, not just knowledge of principles
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess advisory capacity in complex scenarios rather than knowledge recall

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has successfully advised a colleague on a complex copyright scenario (publisher agreement negotiation, AI output sharing, student work IP) with appropriate referral to institutional specialist where needed
threshold_evidence.strong: Institutional copyright or AI intellectual property guidance document authored or contributed to, with evidence of adoption

ai_context: Advanced copyright practitioners develop institutional guidance on the legal and policy implications of AI-generated content, training data rights, and AI output ownership

key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user advises expertly; at Highly Advanced they shape national or international copyright law and policy.
what_changes: Shift from advising within existing law to contributing to the development of law and policy.

false_positives.why_misleading: Advocating for CC is Advanced; Highly Advanced involves formal governance contribution or published scholarly work on copyright
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for formal governance roles with CC, IPO consultation submissions, or peer-reviewed publications on copyright law

false_positives.why_misleading: Legal practice demonstrates Advanced competence; Highly Advanced in an HE context additionally requires scholarly contribution or sector policy shaping
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess publication record and policy advisory roles beyond client practice

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published scholarly work on copyright law, open licensing, or AI and IP; or formal consultation response to national IP authority
threshold_evidence.strong: Advisory role with national IP office, Creative Commons governance, WIPO, or equivalent international IP authority with documented contribution

ai_context: Highly Advanced practitioners are shaping the legal framework for AI and copyright: training data rights, AI output ownership, and what new regulatory instruments are required

key_discriminator: At Basic level computational logic is understood and no-code tools are used; at Intermediate code is written and adapted to automate real research or professional tasks.
what_changes: Shift from understanding to writing; from no-code to scripted; from following algorithms to designing them in code.

false_positives.why_misleading: Advanced Excel use (pivot tables, VLOOKUP, conditional formatting) reflects strong data skills but not necessarily scripting competence
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has written a Python, R, or SQL script for a task beyond Excel; if not, they are at Basic level for this competency

false_positives.why_misleading: Course completion provides foundational knowledge but Intermediate competence requires applying scripting in authentic research or professional contexts
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask for an example of a real task they automated with a script and how they validated the output

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has written and run a Python or R script to automate a data processing task for a real research or professional purpose, and can explain what it does
threshold_evidence.strong: GitHub repository showing version-controlled code for a research project with documentation and evidence of iterative development

regression_risk: High -- scripting skills atrophy quickly without regular use
assessment_difficulty: Low -- directly observable through code review
ai_context: Intermediate programmers use AI coding assistants productively while developing the skill to read and evaluate AI-generated code critically before running it

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level code is written for personal research use; at Advanced complex, well-documented, reproducible software is produced and others are taught.
what_changes: Shift from functional scripting to engineering-quality code; from personal use to shared, reproducible, documented software; from using code to teaching computational methods.

false_positives.why_misleading: Working code at any length does not indicate Advanced competence without engineering quality indicators: documentation, tests, version control, modularity
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Check for docstrings, unit tests, README files, version control history, and dependency management; absence of these indicates Intermediate regardless of script length

false_positives.why_misleading: Introductory programming teaching can be delivered at Intermediate competence level; Advanced computational teaching involves research methods, reproducibility, and software engineering practices
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the teaching covers version control, testing, documentation, and reproducible research practices, not just syntax

threshold_evidence.minimum: Publicly shared research code (GitHub) with documentation (README, docstrings), version control history, and reproducibility instructions following open code standards
threshold_evidence.strong: Published computational research output meeting journal open code standards; or research software engineering course curriculum covering reproducibility, testing, and documentation

ai_context: Advanced practitioners document AI coding tool use in code provenance and critically review AI-generated code as part of their quality assurance process

key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user produces excellent research software; at Highly Advanced they contribute to the research software ecosystem and shape community standards.
what_changes: Shift from producing quality software to building community infrastructure and contributing to the standards others follow.

false_positives.why_misleading: Volume of public code demonstrates Advanced practice; Highly Advanced requires community adoption, citation, or standards contribution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Check whether any repositories are widely used, cited in publications, or contributed to by external researchers

false_positives.why_misleading: RSE role designation is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires recognised community contribution or scholarly/policy influence
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for contributions to RSE community standards, widely cited software, or published work on computational research methodology

threshold_evidence.minimum: Research software that is widely adopted, formally cited, or contributed to by external researchers; or published methodological work on computational research practices
threshold_evidence.strong: Leadership of a national computational infrastructure project, RSE community standards contribution, or widely cited methodological publication on AI-assisted computational research

ai_context: At this level individuals shape community standards for AI-assisted computational research including reproducibility, provenance documentation, and what it means for scientific validity

key_discriminator: At Basic level device security hygiene is maintained; at Intermediate multi-layered security is actively managed and phishing is identified and reported.
what_changes: Shift from passive security compliance to active threat identification; from update following to MFA management and network hygiene; from individual device to connected device and account security.

false_positives.why_misleading: A strong password is Basic security; Intermediate requires MFA, VPN use in appropriate contexts, and active phishing detection
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person uses MFA on all institutional accounts and whether they know how to identify and report a phishing email

false_positives.why_misleading: Antivirus is one layer of Basic security; Intermediate security involves a multi-layered approach including network hygiene and social engineering awareness
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask about MFA, VPN use, and most recent reported phishing attempt

threshold_evidence.minimum: MFA enabled on all institutional accounts; can identify a phishing email from a provided example and explain what indicators they used
threshold_evidence.strong: Reported a phishing attempt to IT security with accurate and helpful details about indicators of compromise

regression_risk: Low -- security habits are reinforced by institutional requirements
assessment_difficulty: Low -- IT compliance systems verify MFA; phishing simulation tests provide direct evidence
ai_context: Intermediate device protectors recognise AI-generated phishing content and understand that professional appearance is no longer a trust signal

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level the user protects their own devices; at Advanced they conduct risk assessments and design security training.
what_changes: Shift from personal security to institutional security assessment; from following guidance to creating it.

false_positives.pattern: IT-literate staff who follow all security policies
false_positives.why_misleading: Full compliance with institutional security policy is Intermediate; Advanced requires the ability to conduct risk assessments and train others
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has conducted a security risk assessment for a research project or designed security awareness training

false_positives.why_misleading: Personal security awareness is Intermediate; Advanced involves advising on new technology adoption implications and designing institutional guidance
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for evidence of formal risk assessment contributions or training delivery

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has conducted or contributed to a device security risk assessment for a research project, identifying specific risks and recommending proportionate mitigations
threshold_evidence.strong: Security awareness training programme designed and delivered for staff or students; or contribution to institutional security policy addressing AI tool adoption

ai_context: Advanced security practitioners assess AI tool adoption implications for endpoint security and develop institutional guidance on AI-enabled threat vectors

key_discriminator: At Advanced level the user advises on institutional device security; at Highly Advanced they shape sector-wide security strategy.
what_changes: Shift from institutional to sector or national security strategy influence.

false_positives.why_misleading: CISO role is Advanced to Highly Advanced depending on scope; Highly Advanced requires sector influence or published scholarly/policy contribution beyond the institution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess national or sector-level contribution: JISC security services involvement, NCSC advisory roles, or published work on HE security

false_positives.why_misleading: Professional community participation is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires formal standards or policy contribution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for formal advisory roles, standards contributions, or published work

threshold_evidence.minimum: Formal contribution to national HE security strategy, JISC security working group, or published scholarly/policy work on HE device security
threshold_evidence.strong: NCSC advisory role, JISC security programme leadership, or widely adopted institutional security framework authored

ai_context: Highly Advanced security practitioners shape national responses to AI-enabled security threats in HE including deepfake fraud, AI-generated phishing, and AI-embedded malware

key_discriminator: At Basic level personal data is handled carefully; at Intermediate GDPR principles are applied to research and professional data collection and processing.
what_changes: Shift from personal data awareness to GDPR-compliant practice in research and professional contexts; from avoiding obvious mistakes to actively applying data minimisation, lawful basis, and impact assessment.

false_positives.why_misleading: Personal privacy management is Basic; Intermediate requires applying data protection law to research and professional data handling about other people
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has completed a DPIA or selected a lawful basis for processing personal data in a research or professional context

false_positives.why_misleading: Training provides awareness but Intermediate competence requires application; training completion without applied practice is a Basic-to-Intermediate threshold indicator
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask for a specific example of applying GDPR principles to a real data collection activity

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can identify the lawful basis for a specific data processing activity and explain what data minimisation requires in that context
threshold_evidence.strong: DPIA completed for a research project with appropriate consultation of institutional DPO and implementation of recommended mitigations

regression_risk: Medium -- data protection knowledge requires updating as law evolves
ai_context: The BI boundary includes AI data protection awareness: Intermediate users check whether institutional AI tools are GDPR-compliant before entering personal data

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level GDPR is applied to personal practice; at Advanced institutional data protection frameworks are designed and others are advised.
what_changes: Shift from personal compliance to institutional framework design; from following DPIA guidance to creating it.

false_positives.pattern: Experienced researcher with multiple DPIA completions
false_positives.why_misleading: Completing DPIAs is Intermediate; Advanced involves designing DPIA processes, advising others, and contributing to institutional data governance frameworks
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has advised a colleague on a complex data scenario or contributed to institutional data protection policy

false_positives.why_misleading: Qualification provides Advanced-level knowledge but practice in institutional governance and complex advisory roles is required to demonstrate Advanced competence
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess whether the person has used their qualification in active institutional advisory capacity, not just examined on knowledge

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has designed a data protection framework for a research project or contributed to institutional data governance policy with evidence of advisory capacity for complex data scenarios
threshold_evidence.strong: Institutional data protection policy contribution with evidence of advising on AI tool data processing, international transfer arrangements, or sensitive data research

ai_context: Advanced data protection practitioners design institutional frameworks for AI tool compliance including Article 22 automated decision-making assessment and data residency management

key_discriminator: At Advanced level institutional data protection practice is led; at Highly Advanced national or international data protection policy is shaped.
what_changes: Shift from institutional governance to national or international policy influence.

false_positives.why_misleading: Senior DPO practice is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires published scholarly contribution or formal regulatory advisory role
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for ICO or EDPB advisory roles, published scholarship on privacy law, or formal contributions to AI Act data protection provisions

false_positives.why_misleading: Volume of institutional contribution is Advanced; national or international policy shaping distinguishes Highly Advanced
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess regulatory and scholarly contribution beyond institution

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published scholarly work on privacy law, AI and data protection, or formal consultation response to ICO, EDPB, or equivalent national/EU authority
threshold_evidence.strong: Advisory role with data protection authority, AI Act working group, or equivalent; or widely cited scholarship on AI and GDPR

ai_context: Highly Advanced data protection practitioners are shaping the evolving legal framework for AI and privacy including foundation model training data, student algorithmic profiling, and synthetic data governance

key_discriminator: At Basic level personal digital wellbeing is managed; at Intermediate others' wellbeing is actively supported and platform design is critically evaluated.
what_changes: Shift from personal to relational wellbeing responsibility; from managing one's own digital habits to supporting peers and designing inclusive digital environments.

false_positives.why_misleading: Personal wellbeing management is Basic; Intermediate requires noticing and responding to others' wellbeing challenges in digital environments
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has supported a peer or student experiencing a digital wellbeing challenge and how; inability to give a specific example indicates Basic

false_positives.why_misleading: Personal moderation is Basic; Intermediate involves critically evaluating the design intent of platforms, not just managing personal use
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person can articulate specific platform design features that undermine user wellbeing and how they have communicated this to others

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can identify at least three specific platform design features that undermine wellbeing and explain why, and has supported a peer through a digital wellbeing challenge with appropriate signposting
threshold_evidence.strong: Evidence of designing an accessible and inclusive digital learning or working environment with explicit attention to cognitive load, accessibility barriers, and notification hygiene

ai_context: Intermediate wellbeing practitioners evaluate AI companion apps and AI-mediated feedback tools for their psychological implications and advise students accordingly

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level digital wellbeing is supported in practice; at Advanced it is designed into environments and policy.
what_changes: Shift from support to design and advocacy; from pastoral response to institutional policy contribution.

false_positives.pattern: Sets digital ground rules in online teaching
false_positives.why_misleading: Basic ground-setting is Intermediate; Advanced involves designing institutional wellbeing-by-design policies and evidence-based training programmes
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has designed a wellbeing training programme or contributed to institutional digital wellbeing policy beyond their own classroom

false_positives.why_misleading: General mental health awareness is valuable but not specifically digital wellbeing design; Advanced requires evidence-based digital wellbeing intervention design
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess whether the person integrates digital wellbeing theory and evidence into their practice and institutional advocacy

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has designed and delivered a digital wellbeing training programme grounded in evidence about platform design and technology-wellbeing relationships
threshold_evidence.strong: Institutional digital wellbeing policy or right-to-disconnect guidance contributed to; or research/evaluation report on digital wellbeing interventions in HE

ai_context: Advanced wellbeing practitioners design institutional frameworks for AI and student mental health including the psychological implications of AI feedback systems and AI companion applications

key_discriminator: At Advanced level institutional digital wellbeing is led; at Highly Advanced national or international policy is shaped.
what_changes: Shift from institutional to national or international discourse shaping.

false_positives.why_misleading: Institutional seniority is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires national or scholarly contribution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for published research, WHO or equivalent advisory roles, or formal regulatory contribution to technology and wellbeing

false_positives.why_misleading: Professional community participation is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires scholarly or policy publication
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess peer-reviewed publication or formal policy advisory record

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published scholarly research on digital wellbeing in HE or formal policy contribution to technology and wellbeing regulation
threshold_evidence.strong: Advisory role with WHO digital health programme, ICO wellbeing provisions, or Online Safety Act implementation; or landmark publication on AI and student mental health

ai_context: At this level individuals shape the regulatory and scholarly framework for AI companions, AI feedback systems, and what obligations HE institutions and AI developers have for user psychological wellbeing

key_discriminator: At Basic level digital environmental impact is known; at Intermediate it is systematically factored into professional and academic technology decisions.
what_changes: Shift from awareness to criteria-driven decision-making; from knowing digital has environmental costs to evaluating those costs in tool selection and professional practice.

false_positives.why_misleading: Basic energy hygiene is a Basic indicator; Intermediate requires applying environmental criteria to tool selection and professional digital decisions
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has factored sustainability criteria into a tool selection or procurement recommendation

false_positives.why_misleading: Interest does not indicate changed behaviour; Intermediate requires evidence of applying sustainability criteria in digital decision-making
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask for a specific example of a digital decision where environmental impact was explicitly considered alongside cost and functionality

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can produce a written justification for a digital tool choice that includes environmental impact alongside functional and cost criteria
threshold_evidence.strong: Contribution to an institutional sustainability committee or working group addressing digital technology environmental impact

ai_context: The BI boundary includes AI energy awareness: Intermediate users factor the energy cost of AI tool use into their sustainability assessments

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level sustainability is applied in personal decisions; at Advanced institutional sustainability policy is designed.
what_changes: Shift from personal practice to institutional policy and framework design; from applying criteria to developing them.

false_positives.why_misleading: Personal enthusiasm and practice is Intermediate; Advanced involves designing institutional sustainability frameworks and critically evaluating provider claims
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has designed an institutional digital sustainability policy or conducted a lifecycle analysis of institutional digital infrastructure

false_positives.why_misleading: Advocating for sustainability criteria in procurement is Intermediate; Advanced requires designing evaluation frameworks and critically assessing provider claims
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person can critically evaluate a cloud provider's carbon neutrality claims using lifecycle analysis principles

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has designed an institutional digital sustainability framework or policy contribution with explicit criteria for evaluating the environmental impact of digital tools and AI services
threshold_evidence.strong: Research or evaluation report on digital environmental impact in HE with specific AI energy cost analysis and recommendations

ai_context: Advanced environmental practitioners design institutional guidance on AI sustainability including energy cost assessment for AI tool adoption and AI infrastructure procurement criteria
