key_discriminator: At Advanced level institutional sustainability policy is led; at Highly Advanced national or international digital sustainability standards are shaped.
what_changes: Shift from institutional to national or international policy and scholarly influence.

false_positives.pattern: Institutional sustainability director with digital remit
false_positives.why_misleading: Institutional sustainability leadership is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires national or scholarly contribution to digital sustainability standards
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for published research on digital sustainability, IEA or OECD contribution, or national net zero strategy engagement

false_positives.why_misleading: Community participation is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires published or policy-shaping contribution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess peer-reviewed publication or formal standards contribution record

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published scholarly work on digital sustainability in HE or formal contribution to national or international digital sustainability standards or reporting frameworks
threshold_evidence.strong: Advisory role with national net zero strategy digital workstream, IEA digital sector emissions reporting, or EU Green Deal digital implementation; or landmark publication on AI energy costs and environmental implications in HE

ai_context: Highly Advanced practitioners are shaping the regulatory and scholarly framework for AI environmental accountability including what disclosure and reporting standards should apply to AI energy use in HE contexts

key_discriminator: At Basic level help is sought after basic self-help; at Intermediate systematic diagnostic techniques are applied independently.
what_changes: Shift from following troubleshooting steps to designing diagnostic processes; from seeking help to resolving intermediate problems and documenting solutions.

false_positives.why_misleading: The restart reflex is Basic; Intermediate involves isolating variables to identify the root cause rather than applying fixes sequentially without diagnosis
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Present a scenario where restart would not help (persistent access permission error) and ask how they would diagnose it; Intermediate users reason systematically rather than reaching for a single fix

false_positives.pattern: Uses Google to search error messages
false_positives.why_misleading: Searching error messages is a Basic troubleshooting step; Intermediate requires interpreting results, selecting appropriate solutions, and validating them before applying
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether they evaluate the reliability of found solutions and test them in a safe environment before applying; Basic users may apply the first result without evaluation

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can describe a systematic approach to diagnosing a technical problem: isolating whether it is device-specific, network-specific, account-specific, or software-specific
threshold_evidence.strong: Documented troubleshooting log or knowledge base article showing systematic diagnosis and resolution of an intermediate technical problem not covered by standard IT documentation

regression_risk: Medium -- diagnostic skills require active practice
assessment_difficulty: Low -- observable through practical problem-solving tasks
ai_context: Intermediate troubleshooters use AI strategically in diagnosis: providing full error context to AI tools, evaluating AI suggestions before applying them, and knowing when to escalate beyond AI-provided solutions

key_discriminator: At Intermediate level problems are diagnosed and resolved; at Advanced systematic institutional problem management processes are designed.
what_changes: Shift from individual problem resolution to institutional knowledge management and systemic failure pattern identification.

false_positives.why_misleading: Being the person colleagues turn to for technical help is Intermediate competence; Advanced involves designing institutional troubleshooting frameworks and knowledge systems
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has conducted a root cause analysis, post-incident review, or contributed to a team knowledge management system for technical solutions

false_positives.why_misleading: General technical confidence and problem resolution is Intermediate; Advanced requires systemic institutional contribution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for knowledge base contributions, post-incident reviews, or institutional troubleshooting framework design

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has conducted or contributed to a formal root cause analysis or post-incident review for a significant technical failure, with recommendations for prevention
threshold_evidence.strong: Institutional knowledge management system contribution that has demonstrably enabled others to resolve problems; or systemic vulnerability identification that prevented future failures

ai_context: Advanced troubleshooters diagnose AI system failures: prompt design problems, output quality issues, model failure modes, and institutional guidance on AI system reliability management

key_discriminator: At Advanced level institutional problem management is led; at Highly Advanced sector-wide systems resilience standards are shaped.
what_changes: Shift from institutional infrastructure leadership to sector or national standards contribution.

false_positives.why_misleading: Institutional IT leadership is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires sector or scholarly contribution to technical problem-solving standards and frameworks
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for JISC technical programme leadership, national research infrastructure governance, or published scholarly work on HE digital resilience

false_positives.why_misleading: Track record demonstrates Advanced practice; Highly Advanced requires contribution that benefits the sector beyond the institution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess sector contribution and publication record

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published scholarly or policy contribution on digital systems resilience in HE, or formal leadership of a national digital infrastructure resilience programme
threshold_evidence.strong: JISC resilience programme leadership, national research computing infrastructure governance, or landmark publication on AI failure modes in academic contexts

ai_context: At this level individuals shape the emerging field of AI system reliability and failure classification in research and education including what institutional obligations exist when AI systems fail

competency_name: Identifying needs and digital technological responses
key_discriminator: At Basic level the right tool is identified and accessed; at Intermediate structured needs analysis precedes tool selection.
what_changes: Shift from opportunistic tool adoption to structured needs analysis; from selecting the first option to evaluating multiple options against defined criteria.

false_positives.pattern: Regular adopter of new apps and tools
false_positives.why_misleading: Prolific tool adoption may reflect curiosity without evaluation; Intermediate requires structured needs analysis before selection
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has produced a tool evaluation matrix or can articulate the criteria they used to choose a specific tool versus alternatives

false_positives.why_misleading: Informal recommendations may be based on personal preference rather than structured evaluation; Intermediate requires documented criteria-based evaluation
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask for the specific evaluation criteria used for a recommendation and whether alternatives were formally assessed

threshold_evidence.minimum: Can produce a tool evaluation matrix for a specific need, including functional requirements, data protection, accessibility, and cost criteria, with at least two options compared
threshold_evidence.strong: Formal tool selection recommendation document with structured evaluation criteria and evidence of rejected alternatives with documented reasoning

assessment_difficulty: Low -- directly observable through evaluation documentation
ai_context: Intermediate technology identifiers systematically evaluate AI tools against formal criteria before adoption rather than trialling them informally

competency_name: Identifying needs and digital technological responses
key_discriminator: At Intermediate level tools are selected well; at Advanced technology needs analysis is led for teams and institutional ecosystems are designed.
what_changes: Shift from personal tool selection to leading team or institutional technology strategy; from evaluating tools to designing evaluation frameworks.

false_positives.pattern: Technology enthusiast who evaluates tools before adopting
false_positives.why_misleading: Personal tool evaluation rigour is Intermediate; Advanced involves leading technology strategy for others and designing the evaluation process itself
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has led a technology needs analysis for a team or contributed to institutional technology strategy; absence indicates Intermediate

false_positives.pattern: Learning technologist with good tool knowledge
false_positives.why_misleading: Broad tool knowledge supports Intermediate competence; Advanced requires designing the technology selection process and advising at strategic level
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for evidence of institutional technology strategy contribution, not just operational tool recommendation

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has led a technology needs analysis for a team or project, producing a requirements specification and evaluation framework adopted by the team
threshold_evidence.strong: Digital tool ecosystem design or institutional technology strategy contribution with documented alignment to institutional values including data protection, accessibility, and sustainability

ai_context: Advanced technology identifiers lead institutional AI tool evaluation processes with structured governance frameworks

competency_name: Identifying needs and digital technological responses
key_discriminator: At Advanced level institutional technology strategy is led; at Highly Advanced sector or national responsible technology adoption frameworks are shaped.
what_changes: Shift from institutional to sector or national influence on technology adoption standards.

false_positives.pattern: CIO with strong responsible adoption track record
false_positives.why_misleading: Excellent institutional technology governance is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires contribution to national or international frameworks
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for JISC, AI Strategy advisory roles, or published frameworks on responsible AI adoption in HE

false_positives.why_misleading: Community engagement is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires formal policy or scholarly contribution
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess publication and policy contribution record

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published framework, policy contribution, or scholarly work on responsible technology adoption or AI governance in HE
threshold_evidence.strong: JISC or national AI strategy advisory role; or widely adopted responsible AI procurement framework for HE with documented sector impact

ai_context: Highly Advanced practitioners shape national and international frameworks for responsible AI adoption in HE including evaluation standards, governance requirements, and what regulatory instruments are needed

competency_name: Identifying creative solutions using digital technologies
key_discriminator: At Basic level digital alternatives are attempted experimentally; at Intermediate structured creative design processes produce documented novel digital workflows.
what_changes: Shift from experimental willingness to structured creative process; from trying a new tool to designing, prototyping, and evaluating a novel digital workflow or solution.

false_positives.why_misleading: Openness to experimentation is a Basic indicator; Intermediate creative problem-solving involves structured iteration toward a defined solution goal
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask for an example of a novel digital workflow the person designed, prototyped, and evaluated; inability to provide this indicates Basic

false_positives.why_misleading: Analogue creative skills transfer partially but not completely; Intermediate digital creative problem solving requires the digital-specific combination of tool knowledge and design thinking
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask for specifically digital examples with documentation of the creative process

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has designed and documented a novel digital workflow that addressed a specific academic or professional challenge, with evidence of iterative development and outcome evaluation
threshold_evidence.strong: Digital solution prototype with user testing evidence and documented iteration based on feedback

ai_context: Intermediate creative problem solvers design human-AI workflows with intentional prompt engineering and quality curation processes

competency_name: Identifying creative solutions using digital technologies
key_discriminator: At Intermediate level creative digital solutions are designed; at Advanced digital innovation is led for teams or institutions.
what_changes: Shift from individual creative problem-solving to leading innovation processes for others; from creating solutions to facilitating creative processes and contributing to institutional innovation strategy.

false_positives.pattern: Creative educator with innovative teaching approaches
false_positives.why_misleading: Creative teaching practice is Intermediate; Advanced involves leading innovation processes, facilitating design sprints for others, and contributing to institutional innovation strategy
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has led a structured innovation process (hackathon, design sprint) for others, not just implemented their own creative teaching approaches

false_positives.why_misleading: Participating in innovation events is Basic to Intermediate; Advanced involves designing and facilitating them
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has designed and facilitated a creative problem-solving event for others

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has designed and facilitated a structured digital innovation process (hackathon, design sprint, co-design workshop) for a team or cohort with documented outcomes
threshold_evidence.strong: Led a digital innovation project from problem identification through solution design, prototype, and evaluation with documented institutional or research impact

ai_context: Advanced creative problem solvers lead institutional AI innovation initiatives with responsible innovation principles embedded in the design process

competency_name: Identifying creative solutions using digital technologies
key_discriminator: At Advanced level digital innovation is led institutionally; at Highly Advanced the field is shaped through landmark contributions and sector influence.
what_changes: Shift from institutional leadership to sector or scholarly influence on how digital innovation is understood and practised.

false_positives.why_misleading: Institutional innovation leadership is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires sector or scholarly contribution that shapes how others understand and practice digital innovation
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for published scholarly work, national innovation programme leadership, or widely adopted innovation frameworks

false_positives.why_misleading: Volume of innovation delivery is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires contribution to the conceptual and regulatory landscape of innovation
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess publication and policy contribution record

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published scholarly work on digital innovation in HE, or leadership of a national innovation programme that has demonstrably transformed sector practice
threshold_evidence.strong: Landmark publication on human-AI creative collaboration in education; or leadership of a national digital innovation infrastructure initiative with documented sector impact

ai_context: At this level individuals shape the discourse on human creativity and AI, and how HE should develop the creative capabilities that complement rather than compete with generative AI

competency_name: Identifying and addressing digital competence needs
key_discriminator: At Basic level personal competence gaps are recognised and training sought; at Intermediate structured self-assessment is used and peer support is offered.
what_changes: Shift from recognising personal gaps to conducting structured assessments; from seeking help to supporting others; from consuming training to evaluating its quality.

false_positives.why_misleading: Training compliance is Basic; Intermediate involves selecting training based on a structured needs assessment and evaluating its quality and relevance
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has conducted a framework-based self-assessment and used it to select targeted training rather than completing everything available

false_positives.pattern: Helps colleagues informally with digital tools
false_positives.why_misleading: Informal peer help reflects general digital confidence but not necessarily the structured approach to competence development that Intermediate requires
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has assessed a colleague's competence using a framework and designed a development approach based on that assessment

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has completed a framework-based digital competence self-assessment (DigComp, JISC BDC), identified specific gaps, and created a targeted development plan with timeline and resources
threshold_evidence.strong: Evidence of supporting a peer's digital competence development through structured needs identification, resource signposting, and follow-up, with reflection on the peer support process

assessment_difficulty: Low -- documented self-assessments and development plans provide direct evidence
ai_context: Intermediate competence developers use AI literacy frameworks to structure their own and others' AI-specific skill development

competency_name: Identifying and addressing digital competence needs
key_discriminator: At Intermediate level individuals assess and support peer competence; at Advanced they design and deliver competence programmes at scale.
what_changes: Shift from peer support to institutional programme design; from supporting individuals to conducting organisational needs analysis and delivering evaluated training.

false_positives.why_misleading: Informal mentoring is Intermediate; Advanced involves designing and delivering structured training programmes with formal evaluation and evidence-based underpinning
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask whether the person has designed a training programme (not just delivered content) with learning outcomes, needs analysis, and evaluation methodology

false_positives.why_misleading: Delivering training is Intermediate to Advanced depending on how the training was designed; Advanced requires the full cycle of needs analysis, theory-informed design, delivery, and evaluation
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Ask about the needs analysis that informed the training design and the evaluation evidence collected after delivery

threshold_evidence.minimum: Has designed and delivered a digital competence development programme for a specific HE audience with documented needs analysis, learning design rationale, delivery evidence, and participant evaluation data
threshold_evidence.strong: Institutional digital capability programme contribution with organisational needs analysis, theory-informed design, multi-cohort delivery, and evaluation evidence showing competence development

ai_context: Advanced competence developers design AI literacy curricula addressing the full range of AI-specific competences required in contemporary HE practice

competency_name: Identifying and addressing digital competence needs
key_discriminator: At Advanced level competence programmes are designed and delivered; at Highly Advanced the frameworks that guide competence development are shaped.
what_changes: Shift from programme design to framework development; from institutional provision to sector or national influence on what digital competence means and how it should be developed.

false_positives.why_misleading: Experienced training delivery is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires scholarly contribution to or formal governance of competence frameworks
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Look for published scholarly work on digital competence, DigComp expert group involvement, or formal contribution to national digital skills strategy

false_positives.why_misleading: Senior institutional role is Advanced; Highly Advanced requires sector or scholarly influence on digital competence frameworks themselves
false_positives.how_to_distinguish: Assess published work and formal framework contribution record

threshold_evidence.minimum: Published scholarly research on digital competence frameworks, assessment methodology, or digital literacy theory; or formal contribution to DigComp, JISC BDC, or equivalent national/international framework revision process
threshold_evidence.strong: Leadership of a national or international digital competence framework development or validation process; or landmark publication on the future of digital competence in AI-augmented educational environments

ai_context: At this level individuals shape the evolution of digital competence frameworks themselves to address the AI literacy requirements of contemporary HE professionals
